automation_evidence.finding: Zero-shot multimodal LLMs were weak at construction hazard recognition: across GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-o1, Gemini and Claude, average precision was 0.31, recall 0.30 and F1 0.30 against an expert ground truth. Best single model (Claude) reached precision 0.42 but recall only 0.29. Authors conclude standalone LLM use for hazard recognition 'may not be very reliable' and call for domain-tuned models. Sample: a set of real construction site images with expert-labelled hazards.

The same hazard-recognition task becomes usable with prompt scaffolding: under chain-of-thought prompting all five multimodal LLMs reached F1 of at least 0.57 (GPT-o3 0.629, GPT-4.5 0.623) and GPT-4.5 recall rose to 0.857, versus roughly 0.30 zero-shot. Authors argue prompt design, not model size, drove accuracy gains - relevant because it means a cheap model plus a curated prompt library can approach premium-model accuracy.

GPT-4o scored about 68.6% accuracy and ~69.6% sensitivity versus an expert panel when judging construction site images, with F1 of 0.82-0.87 and mean absolute error ~0.21 on risk ratings; the authors frame the model as support for human inspectors rather than a replacement, and caution that their dataset was heavily imbalanced toward hazardous cases, which inflates headline accuracy.

Civil engineering students using ChatGPT during hazard-prevention-through-design (CHPtD) reviews identified roughly 40% more hazards than participants who did not use the tool - reported as prior work inside a 2026 peer-reviewed review, not measured in that review itself.
automation_evidence.study_type: peer-reviewed (secondary reporting of Uddin et al., Eng. Constr. Archit. Manag. 2024)

automation_evidence.finding: Vendor-reported: across 4,000+ US MEP contractors in H1 2026, AI-assisted pre-takeoff saved about 6 hours per estimator per month (2 h setting drawing scales, 4 h applying plan-set names); object counting was 60% faster than manual; estimate comparison fell from 60 to 10 minutes (83% faster). Self-reported usage telemetry from the vendor's own product; no control group.

Vendor-published University of Kansas test: on one fire-station drawing set, an AI takeoff tool completed the takeoff in 37 minutes versus 2 h 35 min in on-screen takeoff (~75% time saved), but 36.2 of those 37 minutes were a single user manually correcting the AI output. Single subject, single project - directionally interesting, not generalizable.

A tuning-free LLM plus a construction-contract knowledge base identified risk clauses in real construction contracts with 'solid performance' according to the authors, intended to replace part of expert contract review; no time-saved, error-rate or cost figures are reported in the abstract, so the operational value is unquantified.

constraints: NJ Prevailing Wage Act (N.J.S.A. 34:11-56.25 et seq.): public-works contractors must submit weekly certified payroll records, and since Aug 15 2024 must file them both online through NJ Wage Hub and in hard copy to the contracting public body (NJDOL, 2024).

Certified payroll records are published in a searchable statewide database under P.L. 2023, c.138, with certain fields redacted for privacy - any automated workflow must handle redaction and public-disclosure exposure (NJDOL, 2024).

Public Works Contractor Registration Act (N.J.S.A. 34:11-56.48 et seq.): contractors and named subcontractors must hold a PWCR certificate before bidding or working on NJ public work; fees are $500/year or $750/2 years, and a first violation carries a penalty up to $2,500 (NJDOL FAQ).

Wage records contain SSNs, I-9 data, union dues and deduction details for a largely hourly, often multi-employer workforce - a strong argument for private/tenant-controlled deployments rather than consumer chat tools (inference from the data types in NJ certified payroll requirements).

Bid documents, unit-price build-ups and subcontractor quotes are commercially sensitive; contractors are unlikely to route them through third-party model providers without data-processing terms (inference, not verified in a source).

Work is weather-exposed: 81% of construction laborers report working outdoors in all weather every day (O*NET work context), which compresses the productive season and concentrates documentation work into off-hours.
Federal-aid projects add Davis-Bacon/DBRA certified payroll duties on top of state rules (common industry knowledge; not verified against a primary source in this pass - treat as unconfirmed).
trends: Labor supply remains the binding constraint: ABC's model estimates the US industry must attract 349,000 net new workers in 2026 and 456,000 in 2027, with roughly 3,450 jobs of demand per $1 billion of construction spending (ABC, Jan 2026).

NJ/NYC-metro wage levels sit far above national medians (construction laborers $64,060 NJ vs $47,120 US; operating engineers $89,660 vs $59,850), so each hour of administrative or takeoff time removed is worth materially more here than nationally (BLS OEWS May 2025).

Clerical construction roles are shrinking even as field roles grow: payroll and timekeeping clerks are projected to decline 1% or more over 2025-2035 with about 11,400 openings nationally, i.e. the admin work still has to get done with fewer people (O*NET/BLS projections, 2025).

Public-works compliance is moving online rather than away: NJ's certified payroll portal launched Aug 2023 with 374 contractors and 3,990 payroll records by July 2024, and reporting became mandatory Aug 2024 - a structural driver of recurring, rules-based document work (NJDOL, 2024).

Bidding volume and margin pressure: estimating teams report being asked to produce more bids without adding headcount, which is the stated commercial case for AI takeoff and estimate-comparison tools (vendor framing, Trimble 2026 - treat as marketing context, not measured fact).
caveats: Wage figures are BLS OEWS May 2025 values as republished on O*NET local-wage pages; BLS's own OEWS state and metro HTML tables were not retrievable (the site now serves those through a JavaScript data tool), so BLS was reached secondhand through O*NET rather than directly. No Middlesex County figure exists in this data: the county falls inside the Edison-New Brunswick metro division, which BLS/O*NET report only as part of the New York-Newark-Jersey City metro, so the metro column is a broader proxy. Automation evidence is thin where it matters most for agents: the rigorous studies are about image-based hazard recognition, not about office workflows such as estimating, RFIs, submittals or certified payroll, and none of them measure time saved or cost avoided in a real contractor's back office. The two quantified time-saving claims found (Trimble, Togal) are vendor self-reports, one from product telemetry with no control group and one from a single-subject, single-drawing test. Two items are arXiv preprints that may not have passed peer review. Items labelled inference (bid confidentiality, PII exposure, Davis-Bacon overlay) are reasoning from the regulatory context, not quoted findings. O*NET task lists describe occupations nationally, not how any specific NJ contractor organises the work.

No quantified data found on change-order or claim recovery attributable to AI, so no 'revenue recovered' figure is offered.
